article.headline: A €145 Tool and One GPU Just Redrew the Fluid-Sim Frontier
article.lede: An independent 3D artist has simulated a hippopotamus in churning water at 100 million particles using HydroFX, a GPU-accelerated fluid tool that launched commercially in January 2026 at €145 per year. The result — stitched together across three applications with no studio infrastructure — prompted Blender educator Gleb Alexandrov to call it a generational milestone.
article.body:
Jeremy White, an independent VFX artist, published a *FLIP fluid simulation* — a technique that tracks moving liquid using millions of individual particles anchored to a computational grid — of a hippopotamus half-submerged in churning water. The simulation ran to **100 million particles**, with foam, bubbles, and spray generated simultaneously within a single integrated system. Lookdev and rendering happened in Blender; geometry processing and sand interaction were handled in Houdini. Gleb Alexandrov — a senior voice in the Blender community and co-founder of the education platform Creative Shrimp — called it "a generational fluid sim."

The tool behind it is **HydroFX**, built by Sebastian Schäfer, a German VFX artist whose broader simulation platform Storm was used in productions including *Game of Thrones* and *X-Men: Dark Phoenix*. HydroFX is a deliberate narrowing: a standalone Windows application — not a Houdini plugin — built exclusively for GPU-accelerated liquid simulation. It launched in open beta in October 2025, shipped at version 1.0 in January 2026, and is priced at €145 per year for independent artists. It runs on NVIDIA's *CUDA* — the parallel-computing architecture that allows graphics cards to process millions of simultaneous calculations — and exports to standard interchange formats (Alembic, VDB, USD) that any major 3D application can ingest.

The particle count matters because in FLIP simulation, more particles means higher surface resolution: finer ripples, more accurate droplet behaviour, more convincing *whitewater* — the foam, spray, and bubble layers that distinguish a churning liquid body from flat water. Research-grade multi-GPU rigs hit comparable counts a few years ago on specialised hardware. Reaching 100 million particles on a single consumer NVIDIA GPU, in a commercially available tool priced for freelancers, is the inflection point that makes the community take notice.

White's pipeline illustrates how the indie VFX stack has matured. HydroFX handled the simulation; SideFX's Houdini — the industry-standard procedural effects application used at virtually every major VFX studio — handled *meshing* (converting the raw particle point cloud into a watertight surface mesh) and added the sand interaction. Final *look development* — establishing lighting, shading, and material properties before committing to a render — and rendering happened in Blender, the open-source 3D suite. Three specialised tools, zero studio infrastructure.

Alexandrov has been a recognised voice in the Blender world for over a decade; his courses on space VFX and hard-surface modelling were distributed via Blender Cloud. His endorsement of White's simulation reads less as enthusiasm than as a threshold declaration: tools that once required production budgets are now within reach of a single motivated artist with a gaming GPU and a yearly subscription.

concepts.definition: Fluid-Implicit Particle simulation is a hybrid method that tracks fluid motion using both a Eulerian grid (for pressure and velocity) and Lagrangian particles (for volume and fine detail). Particles transfer information to and from the grid each frame, enabling high surface detail and realistic splashing without the energy dissipation common in pure grid solvers. It is the dominant technique in production VFX fluid work and is used natively in Houdini.

Compute Unified Device Architecture — NVIDIA's proprietary parallel computing platform. It allows software to offload massively parallel workloads, such as particle simulation, from the CPU to a GPU's thousands of cores, dramatically accelerating computation. HydroFX requires an NVIDIA GPU and will not run on AMD or Apple Silicon hardware.

In VFX parlance, whitewater refers collectively to the secondary fluid elements generated by a churning liquid surface: foam (trapped air at the surface), spray (airborne droplets), and subsurface bubbles. Simulating all three within a single integrated solver — rather than as separate post-process passes — is technically demanding and is one of HydroFX's headline features.

In fluid simulation, meshing is the process of converting a raw particle point cloud into a continuous, watertight polygon surface that can be shaded and rendered. Common approaches include marching-cubes extraction and VDB-based smoothing. The quality of the mesh directly determines how convincing the final rendered liquid surface looks.

The stage in a 3D production pipeline where artists establish the final visual character of a scene: lighting, material shading, texturing, and colour tone. Lookdev decisions are typically locked before the final high-quality rendering pass begins.
